newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KLM 96/97 PROFIT SET TO NOSEDIVE.
newsitem.headline: KLM 96/97 PROFIT SET TO NOSEDIVE.

text.p: Higher fuel costs and a hefty wage bill will sharply undermine profits from ordinary operations at Dutch carrier KLM in the 1996/97 year ended March 31, analysts said on Friday.
The airline, which unveils full-year results next Wednesday, is seen posting ordinary net profits of 380-430 million guilders, with consensus at 403.1 million.
Last year KLM posted record net profits of 547 million. The airline cautioned in November that full-year profits before restructuring provisions would be down some 150 million guilders year-on-year.

Including extraordinaries, net profits are likely to be even lower, as analysts expect restructuring charges of 150-200 million guilders for KLM's Focus 2000 programme to boost operating profits by some 1.5 billion guilders in three years.
"On the plus side, traffic figures have improved considerably in the fourth quarter, but yields will undoubtedly remain disappointing," said Gert Jochems, chief analyst at broker NIB Securities.
Results over the traditionally weak fourth quarter to end-March would be dragged down by a high wage bill, higher fuel costs and increased landing fees, he said.
Nor would there be any contribution to earnings from highly profitable U.S. partner Northwest Airlines, he said.
Revaluations of KLM's equity stake in Northwest masked a steady decline in the Dutch carrier's operating profits in previous quarters, but this process ended in the first half.
Nor will KLM book its 18.8 percent share of Northwest profits. It said in February that it had not yet officially been informed of the U.S. airline's return to positive equity.
"I'm expecting a pre-tax loss of some 115 million in the fourth quarter (compared with a year-earlier loss of one million)," Jochems said.
Bert Hoogenhuyze, airlines analyst with brokers Amstgeld, said he saw a fourth-quarter loss before extraordinaries of 120 million guilders and full-year ordinary net of 400 million.
Restructuring charges would likely take the figure 150-200 million lower, he added.
He said that while passenger traffic had risen, much of the increase had been generated by special offers and yields were still pressured.
"The figures in themselves are not that interesting," Hoogenhuyze said. "What I really want to know is what KLM is going to say about its Focus 2000 programme."
Rival airlines such as British Airways and Lufthansa already had effective cost-cutting programmes in place, he noted, with Lufthansa instituting a staff pay freeze until 1999.
